title: Product Management
summary: The core product management interview: product sense and design, execution, strategy and prioritisation, metrics and experiments, and leadership.
tests: Whether you can find the right problem, choose what to build, ship it, measure it honestly and bring people with you.

rounds.title: Product Sense
rounds.focus: Problem framing, user insight and a clear, testable product idea.

rounds.title: Product Execution
rounds.focus: Diagnosing a metric change and making a launch call under uncertainty.

rounds.title: Strategy and Prioritisation
rounds.focus: Where to play, what to build first, and what you will not do.

rounds.title: Analytics and Experimentation
rounds.focus: Choosing metrics that cannot fool you and tests you would trust.

rounds.title: Leadership and Behavioural
rounds.focus: Ownership, judgment and how you work with people.

questions.title: Friendship after a move
questions.prompt: Design a product that helps adults who have just moved to a new city make friends.
hints: Who exactly has just moved? A graduate, a parent with young children and a retiree have very different lives.
What gets in the way: time, confidence, knowing where to go, or safety?
How would you know a friendship actually formed?
followups: Your first version gets lots of sign-ups but almost nobody meets twice. What do you change?
How do you keep the product safe, especially for women meeting strangers?
How would this make money without ruining the experience?
A large social network launches a similar feature. What is your advantage?
criteria: Picks one segment on purpose and explains the choice.
Names the real barrier (for example: no repeated, low-pressure contact) rather than 'they need an app'.
Proposes a solution built around repeated meetings, not one-off matching.
Defines success as repeat meetings or self-reported friendships, with safety guardrails.
Cuts to a small first version that tests the riskiest assumption.
outline: Clarify: goal (engagement? mission?), platform, market.
Segment newcomers; choose one (for example: 25–35-year-old relocated professionals).
Pain points: no anchor routine, awkward first contact, flaky plans, safety worries.
Insight: friendship comes from repeated, unplanned contact over time — design for repetition.
Solutions: recurring small groups around an activity; neighbourhood 'regulars' tables; host-led series.
Choose: recurring small groups (six weeks, same people); explain why over swipe-matching.
MVP: one city, three activities, manual matching; metric: share of groups meeting four or more times.
Risks: safety (verification, public venues), drop-off (commitment deposit), cold start (partner venues).
questions.reference:
I would focus on 25–35-year-olds who moved for work: they have money and evenings but no built-in routine. The research on adult friendship points to repeated contact over weeks, not a single great first meeting, so the product should create repetition.

My proposal is “Regulars”: you join a small group of six people, matched by neighbourhood and interest, that meets at the same place and time for six weeks. The product handles venue, reminders and a light conversation prompt; a small refundable deposit reduces no-shows.

I would test the riskiest assumption first — that people will commit to six weeks — with a manual pilot in one city. Success is the share of groups that meet four or more times and the share of members who meet someone outside the group by week six. Guardrails: safety reports, no-show rate and member satisfaction. Safety is part of the design: verified profiles, public venues, and an easy way to leave a group.

If competitors copy the format, the advantage is venue partnerships and the matching data about which groups last.
pitfalls: Designing a dating app with a different label.
Measuring success by sign-ups or messages sent.
Ignoring safety until asked.

questions.title: Clinic check-in
questions.prompt: Design the check-in experience for a busy outpatient clinic, from arriving at the door to being called in by the nurse.
hints: Who arrives? Think about older patients, people who do not read the local language, people in pain, carers.
What is the clinic's problem — queues at the desk, missing forms, no-shows?
What happens when the system is down?
followups: Half of patients are over 70. What changes?
Front-desk staff fear the kiosk will replace them. How do you handle that?
How do you measure whether the new flow is better?
What personal health data does the flow touch, and how do you protect it?
criteria: Maps the end-to-end journey including waiting and being called.
Designs for accessibility and assisted use, not only self-service.
Handles failure paths: wrong appointment, missing insurance, system down.
Defines success for patients and staff (time at desk, wait-time accuracy).
Considers privacy in a public waiting room.
outline: Clarify goals: shorter queues, accurate data, less staff admin.
Users: patients (varied ability), carers, desk staff, nurses.
Journey: before arrival (pre-check-in by text) → arrival → identity → forms → payment → wait → call.
Key design: pre-check-in link the day before; on arrival, a QR or name + birth date at a kiosk or with staff.
Waiting: estimated wait and a text when it is your turn; no names shouted in public.
Accessibility: large type, audio, languages, a staffed lane always available.
Fallback: paper and staff lane when systems fail.
Metrics: desk queue time, share pre-checked-in, data error rate, patient satisfaction.
questions.reference:
The clinic’s real problem is that the front desk does three jobs at once: identity, paperwork and queue management. I would move paperwork before arrival and keep people at the desk for the cases that need them.

The day before, patients get a text link to confirm details, insurance and forms. On arrival, a pre-checked-in patient scans a code or gives name and birth date at a kiosk or to staff; anyone else goes to a staffed lane that is always open — this is important for older patients and carers. The waiting experience shows an honest estimated wait and calls people by a number or a text message, not by shouting a full name in a public room.

Accessibility is a core requirement: large type, screen-reader support, several languages, and an audio option. When the system fails, the staffed lane and paper forms keep the clinic running.

Success: time from door to ‘checked in’, share of patients pre-checked-in, form error rate, and staff time spent on admin; guardrails are satisfaction scores among patients over 70 and complaints.
pitfalls: Designing only for confident smartphone users.
Forgetting the staff are users too.
No offline fallback.

questions.title: Engagement down 15%
questions.prompt: Instagram engagement has dropped 15% over the last three months. How would you investigate the problem, identify its causes, and recommend a product strategy?
questions.premise: A hypothetical practice premise: the 15% drop is invented for this exercise. It is not real data, and this is not a reported interview question.
hints: First ask what 'engagement' means here and whether the drop is real.
Is it sudden or gradual? Everywhere or in one segment?
Separate internal causes (releases, ranking changes, logging) from external ones (competitors, seasonality, platform changes).
followups: The drop is concentrated among 18–24-year-olds on Android in two countries. What next?
You find a ranking change shipped ten weeks ago lifted ad revenue 4%. Do you roll it back?
Time spent is flat but likes and comments are down 15%. What does that tell you?
What would you present to leadership on Friday?
criteria: Clarifies the metric definition and checks data validity before explaining.
Describes the shape of the drop (gradual over three months suggests a behaviour shift or competitor, not an outage).
Segments systematically (platform, country, age, surface, new vs existing users).
Ranks hypotheses and names the cheapest test for each.
Moves from diagnosis to a strategy with metrics and guardrails, not just a fix.
outline: Clarify: which engagement metric (DAU, time spent, interactions per user)? Absolute or per user?
Validate: logging changes, pipeline bugs, definition changes, bot cleanups.
Shape: gradual three-month decline → competitive or behavioural shift more likely than a bug.
Decompose: users × sessions per user × interactions per session; find which factor moved.
Segment: platform, app version, geography, age, new vs tenured, surface (feed, stories, short video, messaging).
Correlate with events: ranking or UI changes, notification changes, competitor launches, seasonality.
Hypotheses ranked with tests: e.g. ranking change reduced friend content → compare exposed vs holdout.
Strategy: fix what is broken, then respond to the underlying shift with metrics + guardrails.
questions.reference:
I would start by pinning down the metric: is it daily actives, time spent, or interactions per user? Then I would rule out measurement problems — a logging change, a bot clean-up or a definition change can look exactly like a decline.

A gradual three-month decline points away from an outage and toward a behaviour shift: a product change that slowly reduced value, or a competitor taking time. I would decompose engagement into active users × sessions per user × interactions per session to see which factor moved, then segment by platform, app version, country, age, tenure and surface.

Suppose interactions per session fell mostly among younger users on the main feed while short-video time held up. My leading hypotheses would be: (1) a ranking change showing less content from friends, testable against the long-term holdout; (2) users moving sharing to private messages, visible in messaging volume; (3) a competitor capturing creation, visible in creation rates and external data.

The strategy depends on what I find. If our own ranking change caused it, I would weigh the revenue lift against long-term engagement and likely restore friend content. If behaviour has moved to private sharing, I would invest in private and small-group sharing rather than fight the shift. The primary metric would be meaningful interactions per user, with guardrails on time spent, creator retention and well-being reports.
pitfalls: Explaining before checking the data is real.
A list of twenty causes with no order or tests.
Stopping at 'roll back the change' without a strategy.

questions.title: Ship or stop?
questions.prompt: You ran an experiment on a redesigned checkout for an online clothing store. Conversion rose 2%. Return requests rose 8%. The launch review is tomorrow. What do you recommend?
questions.premise: All figures are invented for practice.
hints: What does a return cost compared with the margin on a sale?
Are the extra returns from the extra buyers, or from everyone?
Is there a version that keeps the conversion gain without the returns?
followups: Finance says each return costs more than the margin on the average order. Does that change your answer?
The design team is attached to the new checkout. How do you handle the conversation?
What would you monitor in the first two weeks after launch?
criteria: Converts both effects into one comparable measure (contribution margin per visitor).
Asks where the returns come from (new buyers vs existing, which items, which reasons).
Considers why the design may cause returns (removed size guidance? one-tap purchase?).
Proposes options beyond ship / don't ship (iterate, partial ship, targeted fix).
Makes a clear recommendation with a monitoring plan.
outline: Reframe: the goal is profit and customer satisfaction, not conversion.
Quantify: net margin per visitor = conversion × (margin − return rate × return cost).
Diagnose: which items, which customers, which return reasons changed.
Hypothesise the mechanism: fewer size prompts, faster purchase, less review reading.
Options: ship, don't ship, ship with size guidance restored, test the fix.
Recommend with criteria and a monitoring plan.
questions.reference:
Conversion is the wrong goal on its own: a sale that comes back can lose money. I would convert both effects into contribution margin per visitor — conversion × (margin per order − return rate × cost per return) — for control and treatment. If treatment is not clearly better on that measure, it should not ship as is.

Then I would look at the mechanism. If returns rose mainly for ‘wrong size’ on apparel, the redesign probably removed or hid size guidance; if they rose for ‘changed my mind’, the new flow may be encouraging impulse purchases. I would also check whether the returns come from the extra customers or from everyone.

My recommendation for tomorrow: do not ship the current version; ship a variant that keeps the faster flow but restores size guidance, tested for two weeks with margin per visitor as the primary metric and return rate and support contacts as guardrails. I would present it to the design team as building on their gains, with the data on the size-related returns.
pitfalls: Shipping because the primary metric won.
Rejecting the whole design without finding the cause.

questions.title: The ten-minute competitor
questions.prompt: You are the product manager for a mid-sized online grocery app. A much larger competitor has launched 10-minute delivery in your three biggest cities. What should you do?
hints: Who are your best customers and why do they choose you today?
Can you win on speed? What would it cost?
Is ten-minute delivery profitable for anyone?
followups: Your CEO wants to match the competitor within a quarter. How do you respond?
Which customers are you willing to lose?
What would make you change your strategy in six months?
criteria: Understands own customers and the jobs they hire the product for (weekly shop vs urgent top-up).
Assesses the economics of ultra-fast delivery honestly.
Chooses a position rather than copying (or copies deliberately with reasons).
Proposes concrete product moves and metrics.
Names leading indicators that would change the plan.
outline: Clarify: our share, customer base, margins, delivery model.
Segment demand: planned weekly shop vs urgent top-up.
Assess threat: which segment will the competitor take? Churn data so far.
Options: match speed; differentiate (price, range, fresh quality, scheduled slots); partner for fast top-ups.
Choose and sequence: defend the weekly shop, add a cheap 'top-up' option without dark stores.
Metrics: retention of weekly shoppers, basket size, top-up adoption; watch churn by city.
questions.reference:
Ten-minute delivery serves a specific job: the urgent top-up. Our likely core is the planned weekly shop, where customers value range, price, freshness and reliable slots. So my first question is which of our customers the competitor is actually taking — I would look at churn and frequency changes in the three cities since launch.

Matching speed needs dark stores and a narrow range, so it is expensive and it moves us into the competitor’s game where its scale wins. I would defend the weekly shop: more reliable delivery windows, ‘forgot something?’ add-ons to an existing order up to an hour before delivery, and quality guarantees on fresh food. If top-ups matter to our best customers, I would test a partnership with local stores for small fast orders rather than building dark stores.

Primary metric: retention of weekly-shop customers in the three cities; guardrails on basket size and delivery margin. If six months of data shows weekly shoppers moving to fast delivery for their main shop, the market is changing and I would revisit speed.
pitfalls: Copying the competitor by reflex.
No numbers or economics at all.

questions.title: Five requests, one quarter
questions.prompt: You own an invoicing product for small businesses and have capacity for about six person-months next quarter. Rank the five requests below with RICE, then tell me what you would actually build and why.
questions.premise: All figures are invented for practice. RICE = reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort.

table.unit: Reach = accounts per quarter; impact on a 0.25–3 scale; effort in person-months.

hints: Compute the scores first, then question them.
What does RICE not capture — strategy, dependencies, risk, deals?
Six person-months: which combinations fit?
followups: Sales says two enterprise deals worth more than the rest of the quarter's new revenue depend on single sign-on. Now what?
Your confidence on receipt scanning is only 50%. How would you raise it cheaply?
The CEO loves the dashboard redesign. How do you say no?
criteria: Computes RICE correctly.
Uses the scores as a starting point, not the answer.
Checks the plan fits capacity.
Raises what RICE misses (strategic deals, dependencies, confidence that can be raised).
Makes an explicit cut and explains it.
outline: Compute RICE for each item and rank.
Fit to capacity: six person-months.
Stress-test with strategy: enterprise move? retention?
Decide: build set + what is deferred + how to raise confidence on the uncertain ones.
Communicate the cut to stakeholders.
questions.reference:
By RICE the order is D ({{rice.D}}), A ({{rice.A}}), C ({{rice.C}}), B ({{rice.B}}) and E ({{rice.E}}). Late-payment reminders are cheap and touch many customers; bulk export is solid; the dashboard redesign scores lowest because its impact and confidence are both low.

With six person-months, D + A uses four, leaving two. Receipt scanning does not fit (five) and its confidence is only 50%, so I would spend a little of the remaining time on a cheap test — a concierge version or a prototype with ten customers — to raise confidence before committing next quarter.

RICE does not see strategy. If single sign-on unblocks enterprise deals that matter more than the rest of the quarter’s revenue, its real impact is far higher than ‘3 for 300 accounts’ suggests. In that case I would build D (one month) and B (four months) and move A to next quarter — and say so explicitly to the customers who asked for export. The dashboard redesign waits until research shows what is actually wrong with the current one.
pitfalls: Treating the scores as the decision.
Forgetting the capacity constraint.
Saying yes to everything by shrinking scope silently.

questions.title: Fifteen features or a rewrite
questions.prompt: Your CEO wants a 12-month roadmap for a B2B scheduling product. Sales has a list of 15 customer-requested features. Engineering says the core booking engine must be rebuilt or reliability will keep getting worse. Build the roadmap and explain the trade-offs.
hints: What outcome does the company need this year: growth, retention, enterprise expansion?
What is reliability costing today, in churn or support?
Can the rebuild be incremental?
followups: Sales says a top-three customer will leave without two of the features. What changes?
Engineering estimates the rebuild at nine months. Do you believe it?
How do you show progress to the CEO during the rebuild?
criteria: Ties the roadmap to one or two company outcomes.
Quantifies the cost of unreliability (churn, incidents, support).
Avoids all-or-nothing: incremental rebuild, feature themes.
Commits near-term, keeps later quarters as bets.
Explains what is not on the roadmap.
outline: Clarify the company goal and the reliability data.
Group the 15 requests into themes and estimate value per theme.
Propose an incremental rebuild (strangler pattern) with reliability milestones.
Sequence: Q1 reliability foundations + one high-value theme; later quarters alternate.
State what is deferred and why; set review points.
questions.reference:
I would anchor the roadmap on the company’s goal for the year — say, net revenue retention — because both camps claim to serve it. Then I would put numbers on reliability: incidents per month, churn citing outages, support hours. If unreliability is already driving churn, the rebuild is a retention feature, not an engineering preference.

I would avoid a nine-month freeze. An incremental rebuild — moving the booking engine piece by piece behind a stable interface — lets reliability improve every quarter. In parallel I would group the fifteen requests into three or four themes (calendar integrations, enterprise admin, reporting), estimate each theme’s value, and fund the strongest one alongside the rebuild.

The plan: Q1 commits to the new engine’s core path plus the top theme; Q2–Q4 are directional, alternating reliability milestones with feature themes. Each quarter has a review where evidence can change the order. I would show the CEO two lines every month: reliability trend and progress on the funded theme — and list the requests we are not doing, with reasons.
pitfalls: A dated list of 15 features.
Treating the rebuild as engineering's problem.
Promising dates for quarter four.

questions.title: Measuring a Q&A feature
questions.prompt: A fitness app adds a community Q&A feature where members ask questions and other members answer. Define its north-star metric and the guardrails.
hints: Why does the fitness app want this feature at all?
What does a 'good' question-and-answer exchange look like?
What harm could chasing your metric cause?
followups: Answers grow fast, but many are low quality. How do you detect it?
Someone suggests 'time spent in Q&A' as the north star. Respond.
How would you know Q&A increases retention rather than just attracting already-loyal users?
criteria: Starts from the purpose (help members stick with training).
Picks one primary metric tied to value delivered, e.g. questions that receive a helpful answer within a day.
Adds guardrails: answer quality, unsafe advice, harassment, impact on workouts.
Defines the metric precisely.
Addresses causality for the retention link.
outline: Purpose: members succeed with training → retention.
Value moment: a question answered helpfully, soon.
Primary: weekly questions with an answer marked helpful within 24 hours.
Inputs: askers, answerers, answer rate, time to answer.
Guardrails: unsafe medical advice reports, harassment, workout frequency.
Causality: holdout or staggered rollout for retention.
questions.reference:
The feature exists to help members keep training: getting unstuck keeps people coming back. So the value moment is a question that gets a helpful answer quickly.

North star: questions per week that receive an answer the asker marks helpful within 24 hours. It moves only when both sides of the community work. Input metrics: weekly askers, weekly answerers, answer rate, median time to first answer.

Guardrails: reports of unsafe health advice (this is a fitness product; injury advice can harm people), harassment reports, and — importantly — workout frequency, so Q&A does not replace the core activity. I would define each metric precisely, exclude staff and test accounts, and count a question once even if it gets several helpful answers.

Time spent is a poor north star: confusing threads and arguments increase it. To show the feature improves retention, I would compare members with and without access through a holdout, because members who ask questions are probably already more engaged.
pitfalls: Counting posts or time spent.
No safety guardrail in a health product.
Claiming causality from correlation.

questions.title: Testing a two-sided carousel
questions.prompt: You want to test a new 'recommended for you' carousel on the home page of a second-hand marketplace. Buyers see it; sellers' items appear in it. Design the experiment.
hints: If treated buyers buy more of some sellers' items, what happens to control buyers?
What is your primary metric and how long must the test run?
What could make a 'win' misleading?
followups: Treatment shows +3% purchases with p = 0.04 after four days. Do you stop?
How would you detect that sellers are harmed?
Leadership wants results in one week. What do you say?
criteria: States hypothesis and decision.
Recognises interference: inventory is shared, so user-level randomisation can be biased.
Proposes a design that limits interference (geo or category clusters, switchback, or measuring the bias).
Chooses primary metric and guardrails for both sides.
Plans sample size, duration and a pre-committed stopping rule.
outline: Hypothesis: personalised carousel increases buyer purchases without hurting seller outcomes.
Interference: treated buyers take inventory from control → inflated lift.
Design options: cluster randomisation by region or category; or user-level with a check on cannibalisation.
Metrics: purchases per buyer (primary), GMV, seller sell-through, concentration of sales, returns.
Power and duration: at least two weekly cycles; no peeking.
Decision rule written before launch.
questions.reference:
Hypothesis: a personalised carousel helps buyers find items they want, increasing purchases per buyer, without concentrating sales on a few sellers.

The trap is interference. A second-hand item can be sold once: if treated buyers buy it, control buyers cannot. A user-level test can therefore overstate the lift — part of the ‘gain’ is taken from control. I would randomise by cluster — for example by region, where inventory is mostly local — or at least measure cannibalisation by comparing total marketplace purchases before and during the test.

Primary metric: purchases per buyer. Guardrails: seller sell-through rate, the share of sales going to the top 1% of sellers, return rate and time to first sale for new sellers. I would size the test for the smallest effect worth shipping and run at least two full weeks to cover weekly patterns and the novelty effect.

On early results: +3% at p = 0.04 on day four is exactly the result peeking produces. I would hold to the pre-committed duration. If leadership needs an answer in a week, I would say what we can learn by then (direction and guardrails) and what we cannot (a reliable effect size).
pitfalls: Ignoring interference in a marketplace.
Stopping at the first significant result.
Only measuring the buyer side.

questions.title: Legal wants two more weeks
questions.prompt: Your launch is ready. Legal asks for a two-week delay to review a data-sharing clause. Marketing has a paid campaign booked to start in five days. Engineering wants to ship. What do you do?
hints: What exactly is Legal worried about, and how bad is the worst case?
Is there a version that launches without the clause in question?
Who has the authority to accept the risk?
followups: Legal will not give a clear answer about the risk. What now?
Marketing says the campaign money is lost if it moves. How do you weigh that?
How do you prevent this next time?
criteria: Seeks to understand the legal concern specifically rather than treating Legal as an obstacle.
Looks for options: launch without the affected feature, region, or data flow; move the campaign.
Brings the decision to the right owner with options and a recommendation.
Communicates clearly to all parties.
Fixes the process so reviews start earlier.
outline: Meet Legal: what is the concern, what is the worst case, what would resolve it faster?
Options: delay; launch without the data-sharing piece; limit to a region; move the campaign.
Quantify: cost of campaign change vs risk.
Recommend and escalate to the accountable executive if needed.
Communicate decision and next steps; add earlier legal review to the launch checklist.
questions.reference:
I would meet Legal the same day to understand the concern precisely: which data, shared with whom, and what the worst case is — a regulatory breach is very different from awkward wording. Often the risk sits in one part of the product.

Then I would build options: launch on time without the data-sharing feature and add it after review; launch in regions where the clause is not an issue; or move the campaign start, which costs money but not trust. I would put rough costs on each — the campaign change fee, the lost value of the feature for two weeks, the legal exposure.

If we cannot agree, I would take the options and my recommendation to the executive who owns the risk, not decide it myself. My likely recommendation: launch on time without the data-sharing piece. Afterwards I would add legal review to the start of the launch checklist so this does not happen again.
pitfalls: Pressuring Legal to sign off.
Escalating without options.
Ignoring the user and regulatory risk.

questions.title: A call that turned out wrong
questions.prompt: Tell me about a product decision you made with incomplete information that turned out to be wrong. What happened, and what did you change afterwards?
hints: Choose a real decision with real stakes — not a disguised success.
Explain what you knew at the time and why the decision was reasonable then.
Focus on how you found out and what you did next.
followups: What signal did you miss?
How did you tell your team and your manager?
What do you do differently now when information is incomplete?
criteria: A genuine mistake with consequences.
Clear reasoning at the time of the decision.
Owns the outcome without blaming others.
Acted quickly once the evidence changed.
Concrete change in their practice afterwards.
outline: Situation and stakes in two sentences.
The decision and the information available.
What happened and how you found out.
What you did: corrected course, communicated.
Result, including the cost.
What you changed in how you work.
questions.reference: A strong answer sounds like this (a model of structure, not a script to memorise): “We had to choose between two onboarding flows with only qualitative research. I chose the shorter flow because interviews showed setup fatigue. After launch, activation rose but 30-day retention fell, because users skipped the step that connected their data. I noticed it in the weekly cohort review, told my manager and the team the same day, and we restored the step as an optional prompt after first value. Retention recovered over the next two cohorts. I now ask, before a decision, what metric would prove me wrong, and set up that measurement before launch.”
pitfalls: A 'mistake' that is really a boast.
Blaming other teams.
No change in behaviour afterwards.

questions.title: Disagreeing with your tech lead
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you strongly disagreed with your engineering lead. How was it resolved?
hints: What was the disagreement really about — goals, facts, or risk tolerance?
What did you do to understand their view?
How was the decision made, and how did you behave after it?
followups: Were you right in the end?
What would you do if they had refused to move?
How is your relationship with that person now?
criteria: Describes the disagreement fairly, including the other side's reasons.
Uses data or experiments to resolve facts.
Escalates appropriately, not reflexively.
Commits to the decision once made, even if it went the other way.
Relationship stronger afterwards.
outline: Context and the decision at stake.
Your position and theirs, stated fairly.
How you tried to resolve it (data, prototype, shared goal).
The decision and who made it.
Outcome and what you learned about working together.
questions.reference: A strong answer shows respect and method (a model of structure, not a script): “My tech lead wanted to delay a launch by a sprint to refactor the notification service; I wanted to ship before a seasonal peak. I asked what risk he saw; it was duplicate notifications under load. We agreed to load-test for two days. The test showed duplicates above a certain volume. We shipped on time with a rate limit he proposed and scheduled the refactor for the next sprint. I learned to ask for the failure scenario first, and we now review launch risks together a week earlier.”
pitfalls: Painting the engineer as the obstacle.
'I escalated to my manager' as the first move.
No outcome.
